about: At “Nobis quoque peccatóribus” the rubric directs the priest to raise his voice a little and strike his breast. The prayer asks that God's sinful servants be admitted to fellowship with the Saints. Its list corresponds to the earlier list in the “Communicántes” and ends with seven women martyrs.

s01.narrative: The priest strikes his breast with his right hand and says, with his voice raised a little:

s02.translation: To us, also, Your servants, who, though sinners,

s03.narrative: The priest spreads his hands as before and goes on silently.

s04.translation: hope in Your abundant mercies, graciously grant some share and fellowship with Your holy Apostles and Martyrs:

s05.translation: with John the Baptist, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia and all Your Saints:

s06.translation: admit us, we beseech You, into their company, not weighing our merits, but granting us Your pardon.

w001.function: A dative right at the head, thirteen words before its verb. And these are the only three words of the Canon the people hear, apart from the closing Per ómnia.

w002.function: “Also”, because the prayer before asked for the dead. Now it asks for those standing at the altar.

w003.function: The priest strikes his breast as he says these words — the rubric ties the gesture to the whole phrase.

w008.function: Not the feeling of pity but its exercise — particular acts, hence the plural.

w010.function: The participle agrees with “Nobis” (w001) and “fámulis” (w004): it is we who hope.

w012.function: The “some” is not vagueness but humility: any part at all, however small.

w024.function: Usually taken to be the Baptist, who is named nowhere else in the Canon — the two Johns of the Communicántes being the Apostle and the martyr who stands with Paul.

w026.function: He was missing from the Communicántes, where Paul stood in his room — here he returns to the company of the Twelve.

w029.function: Usually taken to be Pope Alexander I, though the identification is disputed — as with John.

w031.function: Not the apostle: this is Peter the exorcist, whose name goes paired with Marcellinus in the Roman calendar.

w032.function: The name is an ordinary Latin noun — happiness. The analyzers here confirm the form, not the saint.

w033.function: The name of a martyr, and also a Latin adjective (continual) — which is all the analyzers’ dictionaries carry, proper names being outside them. That it is a name here is settled by the list of saints it stands in.

w046.function: From cum and sors, lot: consórtes are those to whom the same lot has fallen. The preposition intra stands before the relative, and the noun it governs only after it.

w048.function: A nominative in apposition to the unexpressed subject of “admítte” (w054) — the reading both translations give. The vocative, identical in form, remains the competing reading and the word carries the disputed flag.

w051.function: A genitive with “largítor” (w053): a giver not of wages but of pardon.

w054.function: The imperative comes last, after the eleven words that precede it.

w058.function: This prayer does not end in an Amen: the sentence runs on into Per quem hæc ómnia.
